items.title: Tokyo 2018 criteria: diagnosis
items.contentHtml:
Tokyo 2018 Criteria

  • A. Local inflammation: Murphy's sign, pain in the right hypochondrium, percussion mass/fist.
  • B. Systemic inflammation: fever >38°C, elevated C-reactive protein, leukocytosis.
  • C. Image: mural thickening >4 mm, distended gallbladder, ultrasound Murphy's sign, perivesicular abscess.
  • Definitive diagnosis: one item of A + one of B + C positive.
  • Suspicion: A + B without C.

items.title: Classic triad and its value
items.contentHtml:
Classic triad

  • Murphy's triad: pain in the right upper quadrant, fever and leukocytosis; present in ~50% of cases, its absence does not exclude.
  • Clinical Murphy's sign: inspiratory pause due to pain on right subcostal palpation; sensitivity ~65%, specificity ~87%.
  • Leukocytosis >10,000/µL with left shift; in the elderly and immunosuppressed it may not appear.
  • Fever >38°C indicates acute cholecystitis, but the absence of fever does not rule out the diagnosis.

items.title: Ultrasound Murphy's sign
items.contentHtml:
Ultrasound Murphy's sign

  • Definition: maximum pain with the transducer over the gallbladder during deep inspiration.
  • It is the most specific finding for acute cholecystitis (specificity ~90%).
  • Its absence in the elderly or diabetics does not exclude; there may be perforation.
  • Combined with mural thickening >4 mm and perivesicular fluid, high positive predictive value.

items.foco: Gallbladder mural thickening greater than 4 mm
items.title: Mural thickening >4 mm
items.contentHtml:
Mural thickening >4 mm

  • Ultrasound threshold: >4 mm suggests acute cholecystitis; >7 mm is more specific.
  • Thickening may be diffuse or focal; asymmetry suggests tumor.
  • Other signs: distended gallbladder (>8 cm longitudinal), perivesicular fluid, intramural gas (emphysematous).
  • Thickening is not exclusive: cirrhosis, hypoalbuminemia, right heart failure cause it.

items.title: Cholecystolithiasis as a cause
items.contentHtml:
Cholecystolithiasis

  • 90% of acute cholecystitis is associated with stones; Impaction in the cystic duct produces obstruction and distension.
  • Wall ischemia due to increased intramural pressure favors bacterial translocation.
  • In acalculous cholecystitis (10%) there is biliary sludge, prolonged fasting, mechanical ventilation or diabetes.
  • The presence of stones does not confirm cholecystitis; inflammatory signs are required.

items.foco: Elevation of alkaline phosphatase and bilirubin
items.title: Liver tests in cholecystitis
items.contentHtml:
Elevation of alkaline phosphatase and bilirubin

  • The alkaline phosphatase and bilirubin may be slightly elevated due to pericholedochal inflammation or edema.
  • Marked elevations suggest choledocholithiasis or Mirizzi syndrome (compression by cystic stones).
  • In uncomplicated acute cholecystitis, Transaminases are usually normal or minimally elevated.
  • If there is cholangitis, jaundice, fever and pain predominate; endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography is required.

items.title: Acalculous cholecystitis
items.contentHtml:
Acallithic cholecystitis

  • Occurs in critically ill patients: postoperative period of major surgery, trauma, burns, total parenteral nutrition, prolonged fasting.
  • Mechanism: biliary stasis and hypoperfusion of the gallbladder wall; increased risk of gangrene and perforation.
  • Diagnosis is difficult: the symptoms may be masked; use Doppler ultrasound or computed tomography.
  • Mortality is high (~30-50%); requires percutaneous drainage or early cholecystectomy.

items.title: Initial antibiotic therapy
items.contentHtml:
Broad-spectrum antibiotics

  • Start empirically against gram-negative and anaerobes: piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g IV every 6 hours, or ceftriaxone 1-2 g IV every 24 hours plus metronidazole 500 mg IV every 8 hours hours.
  • Alternative in beta-lactam allergy: ciprofloxacin 400 mg IV every 12 hours plus metronidazole.
  • Duration: 4-7 days if the focus is controlled; If not operated, prolong according to response.
  • In moderate-severe severity (Tokyo II-III) cover enterococci and resistance.

items.title: Early cholecystectomy
items.contentHtml:
Early laparoscopic cholecystectomy

  • Early laparoscopic cholecystectomy (within 72 hours of the onset of symptoms) is the gold standard.
  • It reduces hospital stay and costs without increasing morbidity compared to the late one (6-8 weeks).
  • The safe window is up to 10 days from the onset, but preferable in the first 72 hours.
  • The Early cholecystectomy is not contraindicated in the elderly; Delay increases risk of complications.

items.title: Tokyo Gravity
items.contentHtml:
Tokyo Severity Scale 2018

  • Grade I (mild): no organ dysfunction, mild inflammatory changes in the gallbladder.
  • Grade II (moderate): leukocytosis >18,000/µL, palpable mass in the right hypochondrium, duration >72 hours, perivesicular abscess, gangrene, emphysema.
  • Grade III (severe): cardiovascular, neurological, respiratory, renal, hepatic or hematological dysfunction.
  • Grade III requires organ support and drainage or emergency cholecystectomy.

items.title: Percutaneous drainage
items.contentHtml:
Percutaneous drainage

  • Indicated in patients with Tokio III or severe comorbidities that contraindicate general anesthesia.
  • Percutaneous cholecystostomy is performed guided by ultrasound or tomography; drains infected bile and reduces pressure.
  • Alternative in Tokyo II if early cholecystectomy is not feasible due to extreme surgical risk.
  • Delayed cholecystectomy is scheduled after resolution of the acute condition (4-6 weeks).

items.title: Complications: perforation and abscess
items.contentHtml:
Perforation and perivesicular abscess

  • Perforation occurs in ~10% of acute cholecystitis; It is associated with gangrene and diabetes.
  • Types: free perforation (biliary peritonitis), contained perforation (perivesicular abscess) and cholecystoenteric fistula.
  • The perivesicular abscess is seen as a fluid collection adjacent to the gallbladder; requires percutaneous or surgical drainage.
  • Diffuse biliary peritonitis is an emergency: emergency laparotomy or laparoscopy with lavage and cholecystectomy.
